paras: The lynching of John Wright took place in St. Helena, Napa County, California, early on May 5, 1888, when a mob of masked men took Wright from the town jail and hanged him from a bridge. Wright had been accused of shooting and killing Budd Vann, a young man of the town, about two weeks earlier, and had been brought to St. Helena for his preliminary examination. A coroner's jury blamed unknown persons, and a Napa County grand jury adjourned without indictments after censuring local officials.

At about 2 a.m. on Sunday, April 22, 1888, Budd Vann, a brother of the St. Helena Postmaster, was shot through the window of a house of prostitution known as the Pink Saloon. According to the Associated Press, Vann and some companions were standing near the house when one of them threw a rock through a window and struck one of the women inside. A man inside, described as the brother of one of the women, fired a revolver into the group and hit Vann in the abdomen; Vann died that night.

The first dispatches named the shooter as "Graham" or "Chas. Graham" and said he was arrested at once. On April 24, however, a coroner's jury returned a verdict "implicating John Wright as the man who did the shooting," and all later reports name Wright. Wright was held in the county jail at Napa until May 4, when he was brought to St. Helena for his preliminary examination.

No one in St. Helena was reported to have expected a lynching attempt. At 1 o'clock on the morning of May 5, Justice Elgin, who held the jail keys, was called to his door, surrounded by a mob and forced to hand the keys over. The masked men took Wright from the jail, and within ten minutes his body was hanging from the bridge at the head of Main street. The body was left hanging and was viewed by passers-by until about 8 a.m., when an undertaker cut it down on the sheriff's order.

The streets were crowded all day with people discussing the lynching, and the Los Angeles Herald's dispatch said it was "deplored by law-abiding citizens." That afternoon the coroner's jury found that Wright had died by violence at the hands of unknown persons and censured the town police for leaving the jail unguarded. No arrests were reported.

A Napa County grand jury took up the case in June but by mid-month had not identified the lynchers. Its report of August 4 censured the St. Helena constable and justice of the peace for dereliction and the county supervisors for refusing to offer a reward, and stated that it had found no evidence justifying the arrest of anyone. The grand jury adjourned without returning indictments.

All of the coverage found is from white newspapers, and none of it states Wright's race. California papers carried the fullest reporting: the Los Angeles Herald headlined it "Sensational Lynching at St. Helena" and called it an "outrage," while the Sacramento Record-Union gave it a single line and later followed the grand jury under "The St. Helena Lynching Case." The Record-Union's report of the original shooting, headed "Poor Bud Vann," had treated Vann sympathetically.

A national wire spread the story east on May 7 and 8, in versions that repeated the account of the shooting and stated as fact that Wright had killed Vann. Headlines varied from "Lynch Law in California" in Waterbury to "A Murderer Lynched in California" in the New-York Tribune and "Hanged to a Bridge" in Yankton. The Springfield, Ohio, Daily Republic printed it as "A Colorado Lynching" despite its St. Helena dateline, and a Minnesota news summary described the lynchers as "a mob of citizens." Short notices of the grand jury's work also ran in Nevada and Los Angeles.

The man accused of shooting Vann was called "Graham" in the first Associated Press reports and John Wright by the coroner's jury and all later accounts; since both descriptions make him the brother of a woman in the house, they may refer to the same person, but no report explains the difference. Wright's first name also appears as "Jack" in Sacramento briefs.

reader.title: Lynching of John Wright
bases: A mob of masked men took John Wright, held on a charge of killing Budd Vann, from the St. Helena jail and hanged him from a bridge (A5, A6, A10).

Wright was hanged by a 'mob of masked men' who forced the jail keys from a justice of the peace and took him from jail while he awaited a preliminary examination for the killing of Vann (A5, A10); the coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown persons and a grand jury sought indictments against 'the lynchers' (A5, A22, A25).

Separate California Associated Press dispatches (A8, A22, A25), the AP Pacific Coast report (A5, A24) and the national wire (A6, A10) agree that a mob took Wright from the St. Helena jail and hanged him to a bridge.

accounts.gist: A masked mob forced Justice Elgin to give up the keys at 1 a.m., took Wright from the unguarded jail and hanged him from the Main street bridge; the coroner's jury blamed unknown persons and censured the town police.

accounts.label: National wire
accounts.gist: Wright, who had shot Vann after a stone was thrown through the window of a house of ill fame where his sister was an inmate, was taken from jail by masked men and hanged to a bridge; no lynching attempt had been expected.

accounts.label: Napa grand jury
accounts.gist: The grand jury could find no evidence justifying arrests and censured the St. Helena Constable, Justice of the Peace and the county Supervisors.

framing.detail: The Los Angeles Herald headlined 'Sensational Lynching at St. Helena', called it 'the outrage' and said it was 'deplored by law-abiding citizens'.
Eastern papers ran the wire under headlines such as 'Lynch Law in California', 'A Murderer Lynched in California' and, in Springfield, Ohio, the mistaken 'A Colorado Lynching'.
Sacramento's Record-Union reported the lynching in one line and followed the grand jury under 'The St. Helena Lynching Case'; its earlier shooting story was headed 'POOR BUD VANN.'
The Kanabec County Times summary said Wright was 'lynched by a mob of citizens'.

conflicts.note: The first-day dispatches named 'Graham'; the coroner's jury verdict two days later named John Wright, and all lynching reports use Wright. Both are described as a brother of a woman in the house, suggesting the same man under different names, but no report reconciles them.
Probably a familiar form; both used by California papers.
The 'citizens' wording appears only in a Minnesota news summary; the dispatches say masked men.
The Springfield headline contradicts its own St. Helena, Cal. dateline; a headline error.
